source.title: Breaking Neural Network Scaling Laws with Modularity
source.authors: Akhilan Boopathy; Sunshine Jiang; William Yue; Jaedong Hwang; Abhiram Iyer; I. Fiete

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws and presents results on generalization versus task dimensionality, but it does not test the listed claim versions about language-model pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or the other specified versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theory and experiments concern squared-error generalization and sample complexity as input dimensionality changes, not held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling or parameter/token/compute allocation. Those dimensionality findings are recorded as related results under fits_no_version. Scaling-law findings cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper's own results are a linear-feature theory and MLP experiments on sine-wave regression and Compositional CIFAR-10. They measure squared-error test loss and sample complexity against task input dimensionality, and double descent in parameters and samples. No power law is fitted to loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Nothing is extrapolated, no compute-optimal split is computed, there is no fixed-parameter shape sweep, and loss is not linked to downstream performance. Scaling-law results appear only as citations (Kaplan, Sharma & Kaplan) and as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that modular networks can, in theory, make sample complexity independent of task dimensionality on modular tasks, whereas monolithic networks need exponentially many samples. Their learning rule improves generalization in and out of distribution but does not empirically remove the dimension dependence, which they attribute to the difficulty of optimizing modular networks.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a theoretical linear-feature regression model and experiments on sine-wave regression and Compositional CIFAR-10; it does not reproduce language-model scaling-law measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The theoretical conclusions depend on the specified modular structure and dimension-independent module input bottleneck. The sine-wave empirical results vary with task dimension and network architecture; the authors report that optimization difficulty prevents fully eliminating dimensionality dependence.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory predicts sample complexity grows roughly exponentially with input dimensionality for monolithic nets (Fig 3). For modular nets on modular tasks, theory gives dimension-independent sample complexity (Theorem 2). In experiments the modular learning rule reduces but does not remove the dimension dependence (Fig 4a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modular networks on modular tasks reduce the dependence of sample complexity on input dimensionality relative to monolithic networks.

fits_no_version.finding: In the toy model and in sine-wave MLP experiments, test loss shows double descent in p and n. Loss rises sub-linearly with input dimensionality m and is invariant to module count k. Theory and experiment diverge at low n and at the interpolation spike.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small regression settings, generalization loss follows double descent in parameters and samples and rises with intrinsic input dimensionality.

record.problems: The evidence concerns toy linear-feature theory and a limited set of regression and classification tasks, not language-model pretraining loss. The theory relies on strong assumptions and a specific form of modularity. The paper itself notes optimization-related discrepancies; several relevant empirical trends are shown in figures without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results were reported. Cited scaling-law results were excluded because they are from other work. Other modular-task comparisons, including Compositional CIFAR-10 accuracy results, do not measure any listed version or the dimensionality-dependent sample-complexity finding recorded here.

untested.parts: Power-law decay of held-out LM pretraining loss in parameters, tokens or compute. The study fits no power law to loss.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
Effect of depth and width at fixed parameter count. Architectures vary, but parameter count is not held fixed and no loss-versus-shape comparison is reported.
Whether a power-law loss form holds in other modalities or regimes. The regression tasks report double descent and exponential-in-dimension sample complexity, with no power-law fit.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The title's 'scaling laws' means sample complexity versus input dimensionality, which the paper cites from Sharma & Kaplan and McRae et al. It is not the parameter, token or compute power law of the originals. All rows are correctly linked to none. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model pretraining cross-entropy scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
The effect of architecture details at fixed parameter count on loss.
Whether the specified power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether fit choices change the specified scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal split, or whether those curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: toy model of NN generalization
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical test-loss analysis as model parameter count p varies.
rows.measure: Expected squared test loss versus p
rows.value: Test loss rises sharply at p = n, then decreases as p increases beyond n.
rows.note: A theoretical result for a toy regression model, not a language-model power law.
rows.check: This is a closed-form theoretical result (Theorem 1), not an empirical measurement. It describes double descent, not power-law decay.

rows.subject: toy model of NN generalization
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical test-loss analysis as training sample count n varies.
rows.measure: Expected squared test loss versus n
rows.value: Test loss decreases as n increases beyond p.
rows.note: The paper gives this as a qualitative trend, not as a fitted power law.

rows.subject: fully connected ReLU-activated NNs on the sine wave regression task
rows.operation_detail: Empirical test-loss trends measured while varying task input dimensionality m.
rows.measure: Squared test loss versus input dimensionality m
rows.value: The theoretical model captures the empirical trend; the paper describes the loss increase with m as sub-linear.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over 5 random seeds; error bars not stated here.
rows.note: The paper also reports discrepancies between predicted and empirical losses at low training data and around the interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: monolithic NNs on the sine wave regression task
rows.size_stated: Various architectures; widths and depths detailed in Appendix E
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical prediction of training sample count needed to reach a fixed test error as input dimensionality m varies.
rows.value: Sample complexity grows approximately exponentially with task dimensionality.
rows.note: This is a prediction from the paper's theoretical model; the plotted lines represent different fully connected NN architectures.
rows.check: The value is a theoretical prediction from the fitted toy model (c=1.15, Omega=1.57, alpha=0.85), not an empirical measurement. The subject should read 'theoretical model fitted to monolithic MLPs', not 'trained NNs'.

rows.operation_detail: Theoretical test-loss and sample-complexity analysis for modular networks.

rows.measure: Expected squared test loss and sample complexity versus task dimensionality m
rows.value: In the underparameterized regime, the paper states that test loss does not depend on m and sample complexity is independent of task dimensionality.
rows.note: The result is conditional on the stated modular structure and assumptions.

rows.subject: modular method, modular baseline, and monolithic baseline on the sine wave regression task
rows.operation_detail: Empirical sample complexity measured as task dimensionality k = m varies.
rows.measure: Training samples required to achieve the target test error
rows.value: The authors state that their modular method generalizes better than both baselines and that its advantage persists at higher input dimensions; the paper also states that empirically it does not eliminate dimensionality dependence.
rows.uncertainty: Figure margins; exact uncertainty values not stated in the text.
rows.note: The figure includes averages over architectures and five seeds; exact plotted values are not transcribed in the text.
rows.check: This row compares the study's own modular learning rule with baselines (sample complexity at target error 1.5). It is a method-performance comparison, not a measurement of any scaling-law version. Keep it only as context for fits_no_version.
